text_blocks.snippet: Several vaccines are produced using cell lines initially derived from human fetal tissue, primarily for growing the viruses used in the vaccines. These include vaccines for chickenpox (varicella), rubella (part of the MMR vaccine), hepatitis A, and rabies (Imovax). Additionally, some COVID-19 vaccines, such as the Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) vaccine, utilized fetal cell lines during production.
snippet_highlighted_words: chickenpox (varicella), rubella (part of the MMR vaccine), hepatitis A, and rabies (Imovax)

list.title: Fetal Cell Lines:
list.snippet: The vaccines mentioned above use cell lines like WI-38 and MRC-5, which were developed from fetal tissue in the 1960s. These cell lines are used because viruses often grow best in human cells, providing a consistent and reliable environment for vaccine development.
MMR: The rubella component of the MMR vaccine is grown in the WI-38 cell line.
Varicella (Chickenpox): This vaccine is also produced using fetal cell lines.
Hepatitis A: Like MMR and chickenpox, this vaccine utilizes cell lines originally derived from fetal tissue.
Rabies (Imovax): One version of the rabies vaccine, Imovax, also uses fetal cells for production.
COVID-19 (Janssen): The Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) COVID-19 vaccine used a fetal cell line called PER.C6 during its production.

list.title: No new fetal tissue needed:
list.snippet: While these vaccines were initially developed using fetal tissue, the cell lines have been maintained and propagated in laboratories, so no new fetal tissue has been required for subsequent vaccine production.

list.title: Not in final product:
list.snippet: Importantly, these fetal cells are not part of the final vaccine product. They serve as a medium for growing the viruses, and the viruses are then purified and separated from the cell cultures.

related_questions.question: Are there long-term side effects from the COVID vaccine?

text_blocks.snippet: While some individuals experience temporary side effects like pain at the injection site, fatigue, or fever after COVID-19 vaccination, there is no evidence of long-term side effects. Rare cases of myocarditis and pericarditis have been reported, typically in males aged 12-39, but these are usually mild and resolve quickly. The CDC says the benefits of vaccination far outweigh the potential risks.
snippet_highlighted_words: there is no evidence of long-term side effects

list.title: Temporary Side Effects:
list.snippet: Many people experience mild, short-term side effects such as pain or swelling at the injection site, fatigue, headache, muscle pain, chills, fever, or nausea. These are normal signs that the body is building protection and typically resolve within a few days.

list.title: Myocarditis and Pericarditis:
list.snippet: The Mayo Clinic says that myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle) and pericarditis (inflammation of the lining around the heart) have been reported after COVID-19 vaccination, particularly in males aged 12-39. These cases are rare, and most individuals recover fully with rest and supportive care.

list.title: No Evidence of Long-Term Side Effects:
list.snippet: Extensive monitoring and research have not identified any long-term adverse effects from COVID-19 vaccines.

list.title: Benefits Outweigh Risks:
list.snippet: The CDC emphasizes that the benefits of COVID-19 vaccination, such as protection against severe illness, hospitalization, and death, significantly exceed the potential risks of side effects.
